L'attachement aux œuvres peut devenir obsessionnel lorsque leur possession prend davantage d'importance que les besoins des vivants, tandis que le désir de préserver un héritage peut conduire à des entreprises imprudentes. Un chef de mine peut poursuivre une exploitation dangereuse pour retrouver un filon perdu, un souverain engager son peuple dans une guerre afin de récupérer une demeure ancestrale et un artisan refuser de céder un ouvrage dont il considère la possession comme un droit incontestable. Les querelles anciennes peuvent également nourrir des vengeances dont les conséquences dépassent largement leur cause première, particulièrement lorsque les familles transmettent pendant des générations le souvenir des offenses subies.

Ces faiblesses appartiennent aux possibilités de leur caractère, sans définir l'ensemble des Khazâd. Leur courage, leur patience, leur loyauté et leur fidélité aux engagements peuvent au contraire les conduire à résister longtemps à l'Ombre et à protéger des compagnons auxquels ils se sont attachés. Un personnage nain peut consacrer son existence à réparer une injustice, préserver un savoir menacé ou reconstruire une communauté détruite, même lorsque les bénéfices de son entreprise ne se manifesteront qu'après de nombreuses années. Sa relation avec les richesses peut être tout aussi diverse : certains prennent un grand plaisir à posséder des objets précieux, tandis que d'autres apprécient davantage leur fabrication, leur beauté ou les services qu'ils peuvent rendre. Un Khazâd peut également se montrer généreux, préférant offrir un ouvrage remarquable à un ami plutôt que l'enfermer dans un trésor dont personne ne profiterait.

Les traditions magiques des Khazâd demeurent particulières. Leur héritage est principalement associé aux arts de Mahal et aux connaissances acquises par les artisans, mais certaines lignées ont développé des pratiques et des enseignements plus rares, notamment dans les développements proposés par MERP. Dans MERP-UI, l'accès aux Professions et aux listes de sorts dépend de la Culture, des enseignements reçus et des restrictions propres aux différentes traditions magiques naines. La résistance naturelle de leur Race et la qualité de leurs ouvrages ne doivent donc pas être confondues avec une maîtrise spontanée des arts magiques, dont les conditions d'apprentissage demeurent celles définies par les règles RMU.

Incarner un Khazâd

Jouer un Khazâd en Terre du Milieu, c'est incarner un personnage dont l'identité s'enracine dans une famille, une Maison et une histoire souvent beaucoup plus ancienne que lui. Son ascendance lui confère une constitution robuste, une longue existence et des dispositions particulières, mais son éducation détermine les connaissances qu'il possède réellement. Un jeune Nain peut avoir grandi au sein d'une cité prospère, entouré d'artisans et de maîtres expérimentés, dont les travaux rythment la vie quotidienne de sa communauté. Il connaît les principaux halls de sa demeure, les ateliers de sa parentèle et les règles qui organisent les déplacements dans les galeries. Son départ peut répondre au désir d'apprendre un métier auprès d'un maître étranger, de conclure un accord commercial ou de découvrir les terres dont parlent les voyageurs. Il peut également avoir reçu une mission précise de sa famille, particulièrement lorsqu'un établissement souhaite développer ses relations avec d'autres peuples ou rechercher des matériaux devenus difficiles à obtenir.

Un autre personnage peut appartenir à une famille d'exilés. Ses ancêtres ont quitté une mine ruinée, perdu une forteresse ou abandonné un établissement devenu trop dangereux, emportant les objets et les documents qu'ils purent sauver. Il a grandi parmi les récits de cette demeure disparue, connaît les noms de ses anciens souverains et conserve peut-être une carte, une clé ou un outil transmis depuis plusieurs générations. Son enfance fut marquée par la mémoire d'un lieu qu'il n'a jamais vu, mais dont les descriptions lui sont devenues familières. Retrouver l'ancienne propriété de sa famille peut constituer l'œuvre principale de sa vie, particulièrement lorsqu'il estime que les générations précédentes ont supporté l'exil en espérant qu'un jour leurs descendants pourraient revenir. Il peut cependant découvrir, au cours de ses voyages, que la demeure a changé, que d'autres populations s'y sont établies ou que les ressources nécessaires à sa reconstruction dépassent les moyens dont dispose sa famille.

Une Naine issue d'une grande Maison peut souhaiter exercer son métier loin des ateliers familiaux, représenter les intérêts de son clan dans les négociations ou accompagner une expédition chargée d'étudier un nouveau gisement. Elle peut avoir appris à tenir les registres d'une entreprise, à reconnaître les ouvrages des différents ateliers et à comprendre les obligations attachées aux contrats commerciaux. Son départ peut être accueilli favorablement par ses proches lorsqu'il répond aux besoins de la communauté, mais susciter davantage de réserves s'il l'éloigne durablement de sa demeure ou des responsabilités qui lui avaient été confiées. Une autre peut appartenir à une famille dont les activités se sont développées au contact des Hommes et posséder une connaissance approfondie de leurs langues, de leurs marchés et de leurs usages. Son expérience lui permet d'occuper une place différente de celle des Nains qui ont passé toute leur existence dans les établissements souterrains.

Un jeune guerrier peut vouloir gagner sa réputation avant de prendre place parmi les défenseurs de sa communauté. Il a reçu une formation militaire, connaît les passages conduisant à sa demeure et sait reconnaître les signaux employés par les gardes, mais n'a peut-être jamais participé à une véritable bataille. Son aventure peut commencer lorsqu'il accompagne une caravane, rejoint une compagnie envoyée surveiller les montagnes ou entreprend de retrouver un parent disparu pendant une expédition. Les dangers rencontrés l'amèneront à mesurer l'écart entre les exercices appris auprès de ses maîtres et les situations où il devra prendre des décisions sans recevoir d'ordres. Il peut découvrir que la prudence et la patience sont parfois plus utiles que la force, particulièrement lorsque la sécurité de ses compagnons dépend de sa capacité à éviter un affrontement inutile.

Le choix du métier constitue une source essentielle d'interprétation. Un forgeron peut considérer une arme avant tout comme un ouvrage dont il reconnaît les qualités et les défauts, tandis qu'un soldat s'intéresse davantage à son efficacité au combat. Un architecte examine les ponts, les portes et les défenses des cités qu'il traverse, cherchant à comprendre les techniques employées par leurs bâtisseurs. Un marchand connaît les habitudes des peuples étrangers et peut se montrer plus conciliant que ses parents demeurés dans la montagne, particulièrement lorsqu'il a appris à reconnaître la valeur des engagements conclus avec des partenaires d'autres Races. Un guérisseur peut avoir consacré de longues années à l'étude des blessures et des remèdes, puis découvrir au cours de ses voyages des connaissances absentes des traditions de sa communauté. Ces occupations donnent au personnage des préoccupations concrètes, qui peuvent l'amener à s'intéresser à des éléments de l'aventure que ses compagnons jugent secondaires.

Un Khazâd d'âge mûr peut posséder une expérience particulièrement étendue. Il a peut-être exercé plusieurs métiers, participé à des travaux commencés longtemps auparavant ou connu successivement plusieurs générations d'une même famille humaine. Cette expérience nourrit ses relations avec les autres peuples, mais elle ne signifie pas qu'il maîtrise toutes les disciplines. Un artisan peut avoir consacré cent années à perfectionner ses ouvrages tout en ignorant les langues étrangères et les usages militaires, tandis qu'un marchand expérimenté connaît plusieurs royaumes sans posséder les compétences nécessaires à l'extraction minière. Un personnage plus jeune peut, au contraire, découvrir pour la première fois le vaste monde extérieur et mesurer combien les traditions de sa Maison diffèrent de celles des autres habitants de la Terre du Milieu. La longue vie des Nains offre ainsi des possibilités d'interprétation très différentes selon l'âge choisi et les expériences déjà vécues.

Le rapport à la parole et aux engagements peut nourrir des situations particulièrement riches. Un Khazâd peut considérer une promesse comme un devoir personnel, même lorsque ses compagnons estiment qu'elle a perdu toute importance. Il peut éprouver une profonde gratitude envers un étranger qui lui a porté secours, ou demeurer attaché à une querelle familiale dont il connaît à peine les origines. Ces dispositions peuvent l'amener à poursuivre une entreprise difficile malgré les objections de ses proches, particulièrement lorsqu'il estime que l'honneur de sa Maison dépend de la fidélité à un engagement ancien. Elles peuvent également contribuer à former des amitiés remarquablement solides, fondées sur la confiance acquise au cours des épreuves. Un personnage peut ainsi se montrer longtemps réservé envers des compagnons étrangers, puis leur accorder une fidélité qu'aucune difficulté ordinaire ne suffira à ébranler.

Ces traditions ne doivent cependant pas enfermer les Khazâd dans un caractère unique. Certains sont austères et réservés, tandis que d'autres apprécient les fêtes, les chants, les plaisanteries et la compagnie de leurs amis. Un personnage peut se montrer généreux avec ses biens, imprudent dans ses entreprises, curieux des langues étrangères ou indifférent à l'accumulation des richesses. Il peut aimer les travaux de précision sans souhaiter passer sa vie dans un atelier, ou préférer les voyages aux responsabilités que sa famille lui destinait. Son héritage lui donne des références et des connaissances, mais ses décisions déterminent sa personnalité. Un Nain peut respecter profondément les traditions de sa Maison tout en refusant de reprendre un ancien conflit, tandis qu'un autre cherche à préserver les droits de ses ancêtres avec une obstination qui finit par compromettre ses relations avec ses compagnons.

Les différences entre les Maisons offrent également de nombreuses possibilités. Un Longue-Barbe peut demeurer profondément attaché au souvenir de Khazad-dûm, particulièrement lorsque sa famille conserve les récits d'un établissement qu'elle fut contrainte d'abandonner. Un descendant des anciennes cités des Montagnes Bleues peut préserver des traditions liées aux relations avec les Elfes du Beleriand, dont les conséquences continuent d'influencer les accords ou les rancunes de certaines familles. Un Nain venu des régions orientales peut appartenir à une communauté dont les usages sont presque inconnus des peuples de l'Ouest, et découvrir au cours de ses voyages que ses compagnons connaissent surtout les traditions de la Maison de Durin. Les Cultures développées par MERP permettent ainsi de donner aux personnages des origines historiques et sociales distinctes, sans modifier les qualités fondamentales qu'ils partagent en tant que Khazâd.

Un personnage peut également être conduit à quitter sa demeure pour des raisons indépendantes de sa volonté. Une guerre, l'épuisement d'une mine, la fermeture d'une route commerciale ou un différend familial peuvent compromettre les activités auxquelles il consacrait son existence. Un artisan peut devoir rechercher de nouveaux commanditaires, un marchand perdre les accords dont dépendait son entreprise et un jeune Nain être envoyé auprès d'une autre Maison afin de poursuivre son apprentissage. Ces circonstances constituent autant de raisons concrètes d'entreprendre un voyage et de rejoindre des compagnons appartenant à d'autres peuples. L'aventure peut alors devenir un moyen de retrouver des ressources, de préserver un savoir ou de préparer la reconstruction d'une communauté menacée.

Les relations avec les autres Races offrent de nombreuses occasions de faire évoluer le personnage. Un Nain peut avoir grandi parmi les récits des anciennes querelles avec les Elfes et découvrir, au cours de ses voyages, des individus dont les connaissances et le courage méritent son estime. Un marchand habitué aux relations avec les Hommes peut s'attacher à une famille dont il connaît plusieurs générations, tandis qu'un jeune guerrier peut être surpris par la rapidité avec laquelle ses compagnons humains vieillissent. Les Hobbits peuvent lui paraître peu soucieux des grandes entreprises, jusqu'à ce qu'il découvre leur courage et leur attachement aux choses ordinaires. Ces rencontres permettent de confronter les traditions reçues aux expériences personnelles, particulièrement lorsqu'un personnage doit choisir entre une ancienne rancune et la confiance qu'il a progressivement accordée à ses compagnons.

Les professions accessibles aux Khazâd reflètent la diversité de leurs métiers et de leurs traditions. Un Guerrier peut avoir reçu une formation dans les forces chargées de défendre sa demeure, tandis qu'un Roublard peut posséder une expérience des voyages, des négociations et des entreprises exigeant de la prudence. Un Voleur peut avoir appris à reconnaître les serrures, les passages et les dispositifs de protection, particulièrement lorsqu'il a grandi dans un environnement où les objets précieux et les secrets professionnels occupaient une place importante. Un Barde peut consacrer son existence à la conservation des récits, à l'étude des langues et à la transmission des traditions de sa Maison. D'autres Professions peuvent être envisagées selon les compatibilités prévues par MERP-UI, les particularités de la Culture choisie et la cohérence de l'éducation reçue. L'accès aux disciplines magiques demeure soumis aux enseignements et aux restrictions définis par le système RMU, sans qu'aucune modification des mécanismes existants soit nécessaire.

Le choix de l'Âge constitue enfin un élément déterminant. Au Premier Âge, un personnage peut appartenir aux grandes cités des Montagnes Bleues, participer aux échanges avec les Elfes du Beleriand ou vivre parmi les communautés établies dans d'autres régions de la Terre du Milieu. Au Deuxième Âge, il peut connaître la prospérité de Khazad-dûm, les collaborations avec l'Eregion ou les bouleversements provoqués par les guerres contre Sauron. Au Troisième Âge, il peut appartenir aux familles déplacées après la perte de Moria, vivre dans les Montagnes Grises, aux Collines de Fer ou dans les établissements liés à Erebor, selon la période choisie. Au Quatrième Âge, il peut participer à la restauration d'ouvrages endommagés, au développement de nouvelles communautés ou aux relations renouvelées entre les royaumes nains et ceux des Hommes. Chaque époque donne une signification différente aux souvenirs familiaux, aux engagements politiques et aux perspectives qui s'offrent au personnage.

La Race Khazâd — Naugrim est disponible durant les quatre Âges de la Terre du Milieu. Elle représente les qualités fondamentales communes aux Nains : leur constitution robuste, leur endurance, leurs résistances naturelles, leurs dispositions pour la vie souterraine et leur longue existence. Le choix d'une Culture précise ensuite la Maison du personnage, ses origines, son éducation, ses traditions et les compétences qu'il a acquises. Les Longues-Barbes, Barbes-de-Feu, Torses-Larges, Poings-de-Fer, Barbes-Raides, Mèches-Noires et Pieds-de-Pierre possèdent des histoires particulières qui influencent leurs relations, leurs métiers et leurs possibilités professionnelles. Les Petits-Nains — Noegyth Nibin, issus d'une histoire différente et marqués par une condition particulière, sont représentés séparément parmi les Races restreintes de MERP-UI.

Avant de valider la création d'un personnage khazâd, le joueur et le Meneur devraient déterminer sa Maison, sa famille, la demeure où il a grandi et la place qu'il occupait dans sa communauté. Ils devraient également préciser les métiers qu'il a appris, les responsabilités auxquelles il demeure attaché et les événements qui l'ont conduit à quitter les siens. Un personnage peut conserver la mémoire d'un royaume perdu, rechercher un ouvrage disparu, poursuivre un engagement familial ou souhaiter acquérir des connaissances que sa Maison ne possède plus. Il peut également entreprendre un voyage pour des raisons plus personnelles : découvrir le monde, retrouver un compagnon, exercer librement son métier ou choisir une existence différente de celle que ses proches avaient préparée pour lui. Les circonstances de son aventure lui permettront de confronter ces aspirations aux traditions reçues et de décider de ce qu'il souhaite préserver pour les générations futures.

Un Khazâd hérite des ouvrages, des serments et des espérances d'un peuple dont les demeures ont traversé les âges. Sa longue existence lui permet d'approfondir ses connaissances, d'entretenir des fidélités durables et de participer à des entreprises dont les fruits profiteront parfois à des générations qu'il ne connaîtra jamais. Les traditions de sa Maison lui indiquent d'où il vient ; les engagements qu'il acceptera, les œuvres qu'il accomplira et les relations qu'il choisira de préserver détermineront la place qu'il occupera parmi les Naugrim.

Khazâd — The Naugrim

Deep beneath the mountain, in a gallery buried far below the surface, a master stonemason examines a crack that has appeared in the vault of an ancient passage. He places his palm against the wall, follows the veins of the rock with his eyes, and asks his apprentice to bring a lamp closer. The passage was constructed long before his birth, when the neighbouring mines still yielded silver ore. He knows its plans, the repairs carried out over the years, and the name of the architect who directed its construction. Having studied the stone, he orders two supporting beams to be installed and marks with chalk the blocks that will need replacing. His apprentice watches him carefully, then records his master's instructions in a ledger whose earliest pages were written by his grandfather. Work will begin the following morning, once those responsible for the neighbouring galleries have been informed. In a few decades, the young Dwarf may himself be entrusted with the maintenance of this passage, by which time he will know every repair made to it and the names of those who carried out the work.

Outside, a caravan of Dwarves prepares to cross a mountain pass. The mules carry tools, fabrics, weapons, and several chests intended for merchants in a human city. A Dwarf-woman checks the seals on the crates, compares the goods with the order register, and speaks with the captain of the guards. She knows the families for whom these objects are intended, the prices agreed upon during the previous journey, and the roads that have become dangerous since winter. Her House has maintained this trade for generations, and some contracts still bear the marks of merchants whose descendants now manage the businesses. Before departure, she hands her young nephew a list of suppliers he must visit and reminds him of the particular customs of each. She hopes to return before the great assembly of her clan, where the reopening of a mine abandoned by her ancestors will be discussed. The proceeds of this expedition could help finance the first stages of the work, provided the goods reach their destination and the agreements are honoured.

In a dwelling in the Blue Mountains, a family is preparing the marriage of two of its members. The parents have arranged upon a long table the gifts intended for the future spouses, among them finely crafted tools, pieces of tableware, and several objects handed down through generations. An elderly Dwarf-woman examines the inscriptions engraved upon a casket she has kept since her youth and explains to the younger members of the family the circumstances in which it was made. In the adjoining hall, craftsmen fit the final pieces of a work commissioned for the ceremony, while guests who have arrived from neighbouring settlements exchange news of roads, mines, and undertakings begun by their families. The preparations will continue for several days, for the relatives also wish to use this gathering to discuss forthcoming apprenticeships, commercial obligations, and matters concerning the maintenance of their home. For the children present, these conversations form part of their education: they discover the bonds uniting their families and the responsibilities they will inherit when they reach adulthood.

All belong to the Khazâd, the Dwarves whom the Elves call Naugrim. Their dwellings extend from the Blue Mountains to the most distant regions of the East, and their Houses have endured wars, migrations, and the disappearance of entire kingdoms. They share a robust constitution, great longevity, and remarkable aptitudes for working with materials, yet their occupations, customs, and ambitions differ according to lineage and community. Some devote their lives to mines and workshops, while others travel the trade routes, govern settlements, study ancient languages, or defend the passages leading to their homes. Their history is that of a people who learned to live in the heart of the mountains, to shape stone and metal, to preserve their knowledge, and to rebuild their settlements after the catastrophes that have marked the Ages of the world.

The Children of Aulë

The origin of the Khazâd is unique among the peoples of Middle-earth. They were fashioned by Aulë, the Vala whom they call Mahal, the Maker, whose knowledge encompasses the substances of the earth, the properties of metals, and the arts of craftsmanship. Aulë desired to pass his knowledge on to beings capable of understanding his works and pursuing their own learning. Impatient for the awakening of the Children of Ilúvatar, he secretly began to fashion the first Dwarves in the depths of Middle-earth, while the world still lay under the threat of Morgoth. He gave them powerful and enduring bodies, suited to demanding labour and capable of withstanding the hardships he foresaw in their existence. He also sought to teach them the first knowledge necessary to understand the nature of materials, for he wished to see his creations develop works of their own and perfect the techniques he would have passed on to them.

This undertaking, however, exceeded the powers granted to Aulë. He could fashion bodies and direct their movements, but only Eru Ilúvatar possessed the ability to give them a truly independent will. When the Creator called him to account for his work, Aulë acknowledged his fault and accepted that he must relinquish the beings he had fashioned. He prepared to destroy them, but the Dwarves then showed fear and attempted to escape the blow. This movement revealed that Ilúvatar had granted them life of their own, accepting Aulë's creations among his adopted children. The precedence of the Elves nevertheless had to be preserved, for the Quendi were destined to awaken first. Aulë was therefore required to put the Dwarves to sleep until the Firstborn had appeared in the world.

The Seven Fathers of the Dwarves subsequently awoke in different regions of Middle-earth, giving rise to the great Houses of their people. The most renowned among them, Durin, awoke alone beneath Mount Gundabad, in the northern Misty Mountains. He travelled southward through the mountains and discovered the valley of Azanulbizar, where the waters of Lake Kheled-zâram reflected the surrounding peaks. In the caverns above this valley he established his dwelling and founded Khazad-dûm, which would become the most celebrated of all Dwarven cities. The descendants of the other Fathers developed settlements of their own in the western and eastern regions, gradually forming peoples whose shared traditions were enriched by particular customs.

The memory of Mahal remains fundamental to the Khazâd. They attribute to him the origin of their people, their first language, and the inclinations that draw them towards understanding materials and creating enduring works. His story also reminds them that the talent of a craftsman brings with it a responsibility towards what he creates. A poorly constructed vault may endanger several generations of inhabitants, while a well-made tool may serve workers long after the death of the one who fashioned it. The Dwarves nevertheless acknowledge that Ilúvatar granted them the freedom to choose their actions. Their heritage inclines them to respect work well done, but it is for each individual to decide how to use his knowledge, wealth, and the time allotted to him.

The Seven Houses of the Khazâd

The descendants of the Seven Fathers formed the great Houses of the Khazâd, whose separation reaches back to the earliest days of their history. Each possesses its own lineages, settlements, and traditions, developed over centuries of existence in regions sometimes very far apart. The differences between these Houses concern their alliances, techniques, institutions, and memories of the events that shaped their people. They do not, however, alter their common nature, for all Khazâd descend from the beings fashioned by Mahal and share the qualities inherited from their earliest ancestors.

The Longbeards, descendants of Durin, are the best known among the peoples of the West. Their history is closely bound to Khazad-dûm, and later to the Grey Mountains, the Iron Hills, and Erebor. They attach particular importance to their royal lineage and to the memory of Durin the Deathless, whose name was borne by several sovereigns regarded as his heirs. The successive migrations of their people have profoundly shaped their traditions, particularly among families forced to abandon an ancestral dwelling after a war or catastrophe. Some descendants preserve objects brought from Khazad-dûm, while others possess family tales reaching back to the settlements of the Grey Mountains or the early years of the Kingdom under the Mountain. Such memories help maintain bonds between communities separated by great distances, even when their occupations and relationships with other peoples have developed in different ways.

The Firebeards and Broadbeams inhabited the Blue Mountains, where their settlements of Nogrod and Belegost played an important role during the First Age. Their inhabitants maintained extensive relations with the Elves of Beleriand and took part in the creation of remarkable works. The craftsmen of these cities were renowned for their mastery of stone, metal, and armour, while exchanges with the Elven kingdoms encouraged the development of techniques and traditions, some of which survived the destruction of Beleriand. The catastrophes that struck the Blue Mountains brought about movements of population and profoundly changed the living conditions of their descendants. Some families joined other Dwarven settlements, while others remained in the regions where their ancestors had worked for centuries.

Four other Houses trace their origins to the eastern regions of Middle-earth: the Ironfists, Stiffbeards, Blacklocks, and Stonefoots. Their history is far less familiar to the peoples of the West, for Tolkien's accounts chiefly concern the events experienced by the Longbeards and their western neighbours. These Houses nevertheless developed settlements, alliances, and craft traditions of their own, among populations and territories whose customs remain imperfectly documented. It would therefore be inaccurate to attribute uniformly to them the customs observed in Khazad-dûm or Erebor. Their members share the heritage of the Seven Fathers, but centuries spent in other regions may have considerably changed their organisation and their relationships with neighbouring peoples.

The MERP supplements have developed the history of these lineages, their territories, and certain aspects of their cultural identity. In MERP-UI, these additions make it possible, in particular, to distinguish the House of Durin, those of Dwálin and Thrár, and the Houses of Bávor, Thelór, Drúin, and Barin. These names and their associated traditions extend the information provided by Tolkien in order to offer players a wider variety of origins. The choice of a House may therefore influence the languages learned, techniques taught, commercial relationships, and historical memories of a character. A Dwarf from the eastern mountains may belong to a community whose customs are almost unknown in the West, while a descendant of the ancient cities of the Blue Mountains may preserve traditions associated with the collaborations and quarrels that once took place with the Eldar.

Solidarity between Houses remains important, particularly when wars or catastrophes compel certain communities to seek refuge among their own kind. Kinship, ancient obligations, and recognition of a common origin may make it easier to welcome displaced families, but they do not erase rivalries concerning resources, alliances, or rights over a dwelling. Two Houses may maintain prosperous commercial relations while preserving ancient disputes, and members of the same lineage may belong to communities whose interests diverge. This diversity should be preserved when portraying characters: the Khazâd Race represents their shared characteristics, while their Culture determines the House to which they belong, their upbringing, and the knowledge acquired within their community.

A Constitution Forged for Endurance

The Khazâd are generally shorter than Men, but their bodies are powerfully built. Their sturdy bones, broad shoulders, and strong limbs give them remarkable strength for their stature, while their musculature allows them to sustain prolonged exertion and work under demanding conditions. They can carry heavy burdens, wield massive tools, and continue arduous labour for long periods, particularly when they have received the necessary training. Their relatively short stature also makes movement easier within galleries, narrow passages, and certain underground constructions, where their balance and stability provide valuable advantages. This constitution supports the activities undertaken by many members of their people, from mining to journeys through the mountains, without determining their personal vocation.

Their appearance displays a diversity that outsiders often understand poorly. Hair, skin, and eye colours vary according to lineage and individual, while the beard holds a particular place in their appearance and customs. It may be worn long, braided, adorned with rings, or maintained according to personal preference and family tradition. Some communities attach special importance to its presentation, particularly during ceremonies, assemblies, or formal meetings, but such practices belong to the customs of individual Houses. Clothing and ornaments may also identify a profession, a family, or an office, especially when members of the same community wear objects fashioned according to techniques particular to their people.

Dwarf-women are considerably fewer in number than Dwarf-men, and their presence outside the dwellings of their people is relatively uncommon in travellers' accounts. Tradition holds that they closely resemble the men in appearance, notably in their beards, to such an extent that outsiders sometimes find it difficult to distinguish between them. This resemblance partly explains the imperfect knowledge other peoples possess of the family life of the Khazâd. Within their settlements, women contribute to the continuity of lineages and may exercise familial, craft, economic, or political responsibilities according to the traditions of their community. Their relative discretion towards outsiders should therefore not lead one to imagine Dwarven cities as societies composed exclusively of miners and warriors.

The Khazâd possess great physical endurance. They withstand fatigue, long marches, difficult temperatures, and certain privations better than many Men, while their constitution grants them remarkable resistance to disease and several harmful substances. These qualities are particularly useful in deep mines, mountain expeditions, and military campaigns, where repeated exertion places severe demands upon the body. They do not, however, protect them against every danger. A poorly supported gallery, poisonous fumes, a fall, or a serious wound may have fatal consequences, and experienced craftsmen know that caution remains essential even for the hardiest workers. A mine master must therefore understand the limits of his teams, organise periods of rest, and recognise signs of danger before an accident occurs.

Their senses are particularly suited to underground life. The Khazâd possess faculties allowing them to perceive their surroundings under conditions in which other peoples would experience great difficulty, in accordance with the racial characteristics defined by MERP-UI. Their familiarity with rock also favours certain observations, but genuine understanding of materials requires training. An experienced miner may notice a recent crack, recognise the difference between two geological formations, or realise that a wall has been worked upon. An architect will know how to interpret these signs to assess the stability of a structure, while a prospector will look for indications of a mineral vein. A young Dwarven merchant possesses the natural characteristics of his Race without necessarily knowing how to design a vaulted ceiling, identify an ore, or direct a mining operation. Professional mastery remains the fruit of education and experience.

Long Life and the Memory of Generations

The Khazâd generally live for several centuries, often around two hundred and fifty years, with some exceeding that age. Their growth and maturity proceed more slowly than those of Men, and they retain their vigour for a long time before the effects of old age become truly apparent. This lifespan profoundly changes their relationship with learning and responsibility. A Dwarf may devote several decades to mastering a trade before being recognised as an accomplished craftsman, then spend much of his life perfecting his methods, training apprentices, and undertaking works whose completion will require many years. The quality of his work is often judged by the passage of time, particularly when he constructs a gallery, manufactures a mechanism, or forges a piece intended to serve several generations.

This longevity gives craftsmen and those responsible for settlements direct knowledge of ancient works. A master smith may remember the circumstances in which an alloy was first developed, although it has been used for several human generations, while an architect may recognise in a hall the arrangements he himself recommended in his youth. A merchant may have negotiated in succession with the father, son, and grandson of the same foreign family, preserving the memory of agreements whose circumstances are no longer known to the descendants of his earliest partners. Personal memory thus becomes an important resource, particularly when it is necessary to repair an ancient structure, recover the boundaries of a property, or understand the obligations attached to an agreement made long ago.

Elders often occupy a considerable place within Dwarven communities. Their authority derives from their experience, their knowledge, and the responsibilities they have exercised, but also from their position within family genealogies. They may direct workshops, advise sovereigns, settle disputes, or pass on techniques whose results are familiar to younger Dwarves, though the methods themselves are not. This continuity favours the preservation of traditions, while sometimes making change difficult. A craftsman who has employed the same method for a century may regard an innovation proposed by his apprentice with suspicion, while a clan chief remains attached to an alliance concluded several generations earlier. Conversely, a Dwarf who has lived through several migrations, wars, or the rebuilding of his home may possess an understanding of changes in the world that no young leader could equal.

The memory of services rendered, obligations undertaken, and wrongs suffered also holds an important place in relations among the Khazâd. A debt may be honoured long after the death of the one who incurred it, an alliance may bind two families for centuries, and an ancient injustice may continue to influence the decisions of their descendants. This faithfulness to memory contributes to their reputation for bearing grudges, but it also explains the depth of certain friendships. A Dwarf may remember for centuries a companion who saved his life, a family who welcomed his relatives during exile, or a foreign sovereign who kept his word. Such bonds lend their relationships a particular continuity, especially when they deal with peoples whose generations succeed one another much more swiftly.

Family, Clans, and Apprenticeship

The society of the Khazâd rests largely upon family, clan, and membership of a House. Genealogies possess particular value, for they preserve the connections between families that may have become widely dispersed, establish rights of inheritance, and pass down the memory of the settlements from which they came. A single kindred may include members living in several cities, separated by mountains or ancient migrations, yet still maintaining mutual obligations at marriages, successions, and collective undertakings. Certain objects help sustain this continuity: a weapon carried by an ancestor, a chest of tools, a commercial ledger, or an engraved stone may recall the place once held by a family in the history of its community. Their transmission is often accompanied by tales explaining the circumstances in which they were made and the responsibilities with which they remain associated.

The relative rarity of births gives great importance to the education and protection of children. A young Dwarf generally grows up among attentive relatives, with parents, family members, and elders gradually contributing to his instruction according to their abilities. He learns to recognise the different districts of his home, the customs governing communal life, and the dangers to which inhabitants must remain alert. Workshops, mines, and transport routes present risks he must understand before being permitted to accompany workers. Children thus become familiar with the signals employed in galleries, the precautions necessary around machinery, and the behaviour expected in places where several teams work simultaneously. Family stories complement this education by teaching them the names of their ancestors, the history of their House, and the events that led their relatives to settle in their present dwelling.

Professional apprenticeship begins gradually, often under a family member or a master renowned for his experience. A young Dwarf destined for the forge first learns to maintain the fire, prepare fuel, recognise metals, and use tools without endangering his companions. A future stonemason discovers materials, measuring instruments, and the movements necessary for precise cutting, while an apprentice merchant studies weights, contracts, languages, and the customs of peoples with whom his community maintains relations. Training may last for several decades, particularly in trades where mistakes might compromise the safety of a structure or the value of an important commission. Masters attach great importance to consistency of work, knowledge of materials, and the ability to understand the reasons behind a method rather than merely reproduce its movements.

Family traditions often influence the choice of occupation, but personal inclinations retain an important place. The child of a miner may prefer studying languages or travelling on commercial ventures, while the descendant of warriors may display exceptional talent for jewellery-making. Some families welcome these vocations, particularly when they lead to the acquisition of skills needed by the community. Others believe that the continuity of a workshop or the preservation of ancient knowledge imposes certain responsibilities upon their descendants. These differences can create tensions, especially when a young Dwarf wishes to leave home to receive instruction from a foreign master or practise a trade for which his relatives had not intended him. The value placed upon work well done nevertheless allows individuals of diverse origins to gain a reputation founded upon their achievements.

Marriages are relatively rare and generally enduring. Some Khazâd choose to remain unmarried, either from personal inclination or because they never encounter someone whom they wish to wed, while others devote a substantial part of their lives to their families and the upbringing of their children. Women contribute to the continuity of lineages and the preservation of settlements, although their activities remain imperfectly known to outsiders. According to House and tradition, they may assume familial, economic, craft, or political responsibilities, particularly in communities where relations between great kindreds hold an important place. Marriages may bring families closer, contribute to the transmission of property, and strengthen ancient obligations, but personal choices and feelings remain essential to the lives of those concerned.

The authority of elders, clan chiefs, and sovereigns forms part of this family organisation. A Dwarven king embodies the continuity of his lineage, the protection of the dwellings, and the preservation of his people's rights. He must oversee resources, works, relations with other Houses, and the defence of the settlements entrusted to his care. Clan chiefs may play an important role in distributing activities, settling disputes, or deciding matters concerning a collective undertaking. This understanding of power may produce rulers capable of devoting their long lives to the prosperity of their subjects, but it may also nourish succession disputes and rivalries between families. Ownership of a mine, control of a passage, or rights over an abandoned dwelling may give rise to conflicts lasting longer than several human generations.

Life Beneath the Mountain

The great dwellings of the Khazâd are among the most remarkable achievements in Middle-earth. They are true settlements, bringing together homes, workshops, stores, reserves, passageways, meeting places, and defensive works within a complex designed to endure. Their construction requires a thorough knowledge of the mountain, for architects must study the quality of the rock, the movement of water, natural passages, and the possibilities for extraction before beginning their work. Galleries must allow materials to be transported, rubble to be removed, and inhabitants to move freely, while the deepest districts require arrangements for renewing the air and draining water. The soundness of the whole depends upon regular inspection, particularly when new workings are opened near older structures.

Light and warmth are essential concerns. Lamps, hearths, and lighting arrangements are distributed according to the inhabitants' needs, while some dwellings possess openings cut through the mountain to bring daylight into the inner halls. Workshops where metal is worked must be arranged to carry away fumes and protect passages frequented by families, while food stores require conditions suited to preserving provisions. Great cities sometimes possess underground roads connecting distant districts, or even opposite sides of the same mountain, allowing goods to be transported under shelter from the weather. These routes require constant maintenance, for a collapse, water infiltration, or the deterioration of supporting structures may interrupt the activities of several neighbourhoods.

Great halls accommodate assemblies, ceremonies, communal meals, and receptions held for distinguished visitors. Their dimensions allow representatives of several families, or even of an entire House, to gather together, while pillars, inscriptions, and sculptures often recall the sovereigns and craftsmen associated with their construction. Private dwellings are more modest in arrangement, adapted to the needs of families and the resources of the community. Some contain several rooms connected by a common passage, with spaces reserved for rest, food preparation, and the storage of possessions. Family workshops may occupy adjoining rooms, particularly when their activities produce little smoke or noise. Districts devoted to more demanding labour are generally established in areas where the necessary routes and installations can be provided without disturbing the peace of the inhabitants.

Daily life rests upon careful organisation. Guards watch the entrances, those responsible for stores monitor provisions, craftsmen maintain communal tools, and teams of workers regularly inspect the galleries. Kitchens prepare meals, carriers move goods between workshops and warehouses, while those responsible for each district ensure that the necessary resources remain available. Children attend the places suited to their instruction and gradually learn to recognise passages reserved for workers. Elders may devote part of their time to advising officials, teaching their craft, or examining the records that preserve the history of earlier works. In such a city, every activity depends upon many others, and the quality of the most prestigious constructions rests upon the regular labour of those who provide for the ordinary necessities of the community.

Not every Dwarven dwelling, however, possesses the grandeur of Khazad-dûm or Erebor. Small mining communities, fortified settlements, villages established near the mountains, and merchants' houses also form part of their world. Some Khazâd spend much of their lives upon the roads, in foreign trading posts, or among peoples with whom their House maintains enduring relations. Others live within communities displaced after the destruction of an ancient dwelling, preserving only part of the works and traditions of their ancestors. These varied circumstances profoundly influence the education of characters, for a young Dwarf raised in a great underground city does not necessarily possess the same knowledge as a child who grew up among travellers or in an isolated mountain settlement.

The Crafts of Mahal

Working with materials holds a central place in the traditions of the Khazâd. The knowledge inherited from Mahal nourishes their aptitude for understanding the properties of stone, ores, and metals, but true mastery results from long and demanding training. Dwarves place great value upon precision, soundness, and quality of workmanship, particularly when their creations are intended to serve for several generations. A craftsman must know the materials he uses, understand the stresses to which his work will be subjected, and foresee the means necessary for its maintenance. This exacting attitude favours the transmission of techniques, the preservation of tools, and respect for masters whose experience helps prevent costly mistakes. It does not concern only prestigious creations, for the quality of a lock, hinge, or ordinary instrument may be of considerable importance in a city whose inhabitants depend upon their equipment.

Mining calls upon many complementary trades. Prospectors search for veins and assess the nature of the ground, while miners open galleries and extract materials. Support crews ensure the stability of passages, carriers transport ore to places where it is processed, and those directing the work must organise teams, supervise reserves, and determine whether an operation remains sufficiently productive. Opening a new mine is a considerable undertaking, particularly when the vein lies in a region difficult to reach or the galleries must pass through unstable rock formations. Decisions then require a thorough understanding of risks and available resources, for a poorly planned operation may endanger the workers and lead to the loss of works undertaken over several decades.

Smelters and smiths then transform ores into tools, weapons, armour, and parts required for construction. The quality of their work depends upon the choice of materials, mastery of temperatures, shaping, and the treatments applied to the metal. Some workshops manufacture ordinary objects essential to daily life, while others produce weapons, protective equipment, or particularly elaborate pieces intended for sovereigns and foreign patrons. Stonemasons, architects, and engineers possess complementary skills. They design stairways, bridges, fortifications, and great halls whose stability must be maintained over long periods, taking account of the properties of the rock and the constraints imposed by neighbouring structures. Their knowledge rests upon observation, measurement, and experience gained from earlier building projects.

Jewellers seek other qualities. They select gems according to their clarity, colour, and shape, work precious metals, and design settings capable of protecting the stones while enhancing their beauty. Their creations may possess considerable economic, familial, or symbolic value, particularly when they become the emblems of a lineage or commemorate an undertaking concluded between several Houses. The Khazâd also excel in occupations less celebrated but essential to the prosperity of their settlements: woodworking, maintaining mechanisms, making clothing, preparing food, transport, and commerce. A city may possess the richest mines in its region and nevertheless experience grave difficulties if its supplies are interrupted or if the craftsmen responsible for maintaining its installations can no longer obtain the necessary materials.

Professional secrets hold an important place in certain traditions. A forging method, a stonecutting technique, or the location of a mineral vein may represent a valuable advantage, passed on only to family members or apprentices who have earned the confidence of a master. This reserve protects knowledge accumulated over generations, but may also provoke rivalry when several workshops seek the same commission or an invention challenges established methods. Exceptional works sometimes acquire a significance exceeding their original purpose: a suit of armour recalls a victory, a necklace becomes the emblem of a lineage, and a door bears witness to an ancient alliance. Their loss may then represent much more than material damage, for it deprives a family of an object to which part of its history remains attached.

Commerce, Roads, and Relations Between Peoples

The Khazâd maintain extensive relations with other peoples, chiefly through commerce, the exchange of knowledge, and the defence of common interests. Their dwellings produce highly sought-after objects, ranging from tools and weapons to jewellery, metalwork, and components needed for great constructions. In return, Dwarven communities may require foodstuffs, timber, textiles, livestock, and other resources more readily obtained in cultivated lands. Trade therefore encourages lasting relationships between underground settlements and neighbouring populations, particularly when the roads remain safe and commercial agreements are honoured.

Dwarven merchants often possess a thorough knowledge of the families and communities with whom they trade. Their long lives allow them personally to remember contracts concluded several generations earlier, and some traders may have negotiated in succession with the ancestors of their present partners. This continuity encourages trust when obligations are honoured, but may also make disputes difficult to settle. An unpaid debt, defective merchandise, or a disagreement concerning ownership of a mineral vein may leave lasting marks upon relations between two communities. The Khazâd generally appreciate precise contracts and faithfulness to one's word, particularly when exchanges require considerable investment or involve the responsibility of several families.

Commerce, however, demands far more than the manufacture of high-quality goods. Caravans must be organised, animals fed, and routes chosen according to the seasons and the dangers encountered. A merchant must know the customs of the populations he meets, understand their units of measurement, and recognise the authorities with whom agreements must be concluded. Dwarves accustomed to travel may therefore speak several languages, frequent foreign courts, and know the political difficulties of regions far removed from their homes. Some establish permanent trading posts in human cities, while others prefer regularly to accompany the same caravans. Their children may grow up among several peoples and develop a familiarity with foreign customs much greater than that of relatives who remained in the mountains.

Commercial relationships also encourage the exchange of knowledge. Dwarven craftsmen may work alongside Elven masters, take part in constructing works commissioned by human sovereigns, or teach certain techniques to foreign collaborators. Such undertakings nevertheless require deciding which knowledge may be shared and which families wish to preserve. A master may agree to manufacture an object for a patron while refusing to reveal the processes employed in his workshop. This reserve sometimes contributes to their reputation as a secretive people, but it belongs to an understanding of professional responsibility in which passing on knowledge constitutes an important commitment. A Dwarf may therefore be entirely honest in his dealings, scrupulously honour his contracts, and nevertheless preserve the secrets of his House.

Speech, Names, and Secrets

The Khazâd possess their own language, Khuzdul, which Aulë taught to their earliest ancestors. They preserve it with remarkable discretion and rarely reveal it to outsiders, particularly when it concerns the most personal forms of their speech. This reserve helps maintain considerable linguistic continuity, sustained by the care taken to preserve ancient words and expressions associated with lineages, dwellings, and works. Differences between Houses and changes particular to different Ages may enrich its use, but the desire to preserve this heritage remains an important aspect of their identity. Khuzdul thus constitutes a bond between communities separated by great distances and whose relations with other peoples have sometimes profoundly changed their everyday customs.

The true names of the Khazâd belong to this language and generally remain secret. They are not revealed to foreign peoples and may remain unknown even to individuals who have maintained close relations with their bearers for many years. In trade, travel, and diplomatic relations, Dwarves readily employ names borrowed from the languages of their neighbours, and these may remain in use throughout their lives. A merchant known by a human name may therefore bear another among his own people, associated with his family and personal history. This distinction between the intimate and public name holds a particular place in their understanding of identity, and funerary customs likewise respect the secrecy attached to true names.

Dwarves employ writing systems suited to the materials and activities of their people. The Cirth, whose origins lie among the Elves, were widely adopted for engraving inscriptions upon stone and metal, for their shapes are particularly well suited to the work of the chisel. They make it possible to preserve names, warnings, documents, and accounts intended to survive for centuries. In underground dwellings, inscriptions may indicate the purpose of a passage, recall the dangers of an ancient working, or preserve the names of craftsmen associated with a construction. The Khazâd may also employ signs and discreet means of communication, particularly when the noise of a workshop, the requirements of a patrol, or the distance between two workers makes speech difficult.

This linguistic reserve does not prevent the learning of foreign languages. Dwarven merchants, diplomats, and travellers may know several human tongues, understand certain Elven expressions, and adapt their manner of speaking to the customs of the communities they visit. An experienced trader may negotiate with representatives of several peoples without ever revealing the secrets of his ancestral language, while a craftsman who has worked among Elves may know the technical terms required for their collaboration. These differences depend upon education and personal experience. A young Dwarf raised in an isolated dwelling possesses his linguistic heritage without necessarily being able to converse with the peoples of the West, while a traveller accustomed to foreign markets may have acquired considerable knowledge during his expeditions.

Mahal, the Ancestors, and the Fate of the Dwarves

The Khazâd acknowledge Eru Ilúvatar as the supreme Creator and hold Mahal in profound reverence, for he fashioned their earliest ancestors and passed on the teachings that laid the foundations of their people. The memory of this origin holds an important place in their traditions, particularly through the tales of the Seven Fathers, the founding of the Houses, and the great works accomplished by earlier generations. Their relationship with Mahal finds expression especially in the respect accorded to work well done, for the making of an object engages the responsibility of its creator. A master may remind his apprentice that the soundness of a vault, the quality of a tool, or the precision of a mechanism bears witness as much to consideration for others as to the craftsman's skill.

The memory of ancestors is closely bound to the preservation of dwellings and works. Tombs occupy a particular place in Dwarven settlements, where sovereigns and figures of great renown may rest in carefully prepared burial places. Inscriptions recall their lineages, achievements, and the events with which they were associated, while families maintain places of remembrance and strive to preserve the names of those who came before them. Ancient halls may also retain sculptures, objects, or documents bearing witness to works carried out by several generations. This faithfulness explains the particular sorrow that may accompany the abandonment of an ancestral dwelling, for such a loss often means separation from the tombs, works, and material memories that connect the living with their predecessors.

The Khazâd also possess their own beliefs concerning death. According to their traditions, Mahal gathers their spirits in halls reserved for them within the Halls of Mandos, where they await a destiny distinct from that of Elves and Men. They also cherish the hope of taking part, after the end of the world, in the restoration of Arda alongside their Maker. This belief lends particular significance to their attachment to enduring works: kingdoms may fall, mines may be exhausted, and cities may be destroyed, yet the Dwarves consider their efforts to form part of a greater history. Their faithfulness to ancient works and inherited obligations may thus be understood as a means of preserving the continuity of their people despite the catastrophes that have marked their existence.

These traditions nevertheless impose no single personality. Some Khazâd are deeply attached to the tales of Mahal and the customs of their ancestors, while others place greater importance upon the immediate responsibilities of family and occupation. A character may seek to understand the beliefs of other peoples, harbour doubts concerning certain teachings, or consider that the finest tribute to his predecessors is to continue the work they began. Spiritual practices must also be distinguished from the magical arts, whose mastery rests upon particular teachings and dispositions. The knowledge of craftsmen, ancient traditions, and reverence for Mahal grant no automatic access to the powers defined by RMU rules.

From Glorious Kingdoms to Long Migrations

The history of the Khazâd is marked as much by the greatness of their settlements as by the catastrophes that forced them to abandon them. During the First Age, the cities of Nogrod and Belegost prospered in the Blue Mountains, where their inhabitants maintained important commercial relations with the Elves of Beleriand. Their craftsmen participated in the creation of remarkable works, particularly in stone, metal, and armour. Collaboration with the Elven kingdoms allowed exchanges of knowledge and encouraged relationships, some of which endured for generations. These alliances nevertheless suffered tragic ruptures, notably during the events surrounding the Nauglamír and Thingol's Silmaril, which led to the death of the king of Doriath and renewed conflict between the peoples. The memory of these struggles contributed to enduring mistrust among certain lineages, while the upheavals at the end of the First Age profoundly transformed the settlements of the Blue Mountains.

Meanwhile, Khazad-dûm grew beneath the Misty Mountains. The dwelling founded by Durin became an immense city, renowned for its halls, stonework, and mineral wealth, to which the mining of mithril brought considerable prosperity. During the Second Age, the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm maintained particularly fruitful relations with the Elves of Eregion, whose craftsmen shared their interest in fine workmanship and the properties of materials. This closeness encouraged great collaborations and allowed the two peoples to exchange precious knowledge. When Sauron ravaged Eregion, the Dwarves took part in the resistance and welcomed some of the survivors, while their own dwellings gradually had to adapt to the threats gathering over the surrounding lands.

Yet the great upheavals eventually reached their mightiest city. During the Third Age, the miners of Khazad-dûm awakened a Balrog that had lain hidden in the depths since the ancient wars. The death of Durin VI, followed by that of his successor Náin I, led to the abandonment of the city, which other peoples thereafter knew as Moria. This catastrophe scattered many families, whose members were forced to seek refuge in other settlements while preserving the memory of their lost home. The Longbeards established themselves successively in several northern regions, particularly at Erebor and in the Grey Mountains, where they developed new mines and workshops. The attacks of Dragons, however, brought further migrations, recalling how accumulated wealth could attract enemies capable of destroying the works of generations.

The destruction of the Kingdom under the Mountain by Smaug brought about another scattering of Durin's people. Some families travelled to the Blue Mountains, others remained in the Iron Hills, while still others continued their activities in more modest communities. The descendants of the exiles nevertheless preserved the memory of Erebor and the rights they believed they held over its riches, passing on to their children tales of a dwelling that many of them had never seen. The recovery of Erebor and the events surrounding the Battle of Five Armies finally made possible the restoration of the Kingdom under the Mountain, but this victory did not end the dangers to which the Khazâd remained exposed. During the War of the Ring, the Dwarves once more had to defend their lands against Sauron's forces, particularly in the northern regions where the fighting also affected the kingdoms of Men.

During the Fourth Age, their communities continue their activities and take part in rebuilding territories damaged by war. Some ancient dwellings recover considerable prosperity, while new enterprises are undertaken in regions hitherto little exploited. Dwarven craftsmen contribute to restoring damaged structures and maintain renewed relationships with the kingdoms of Men. For the Khazâd, this succession of foundations, losses, and returns forms an essential part of their memory. A character may belong to a family established for centuries in the same mountain, while another descends from exiles who preserve tales of a kingdom whose great halls no living member of the family has ever seen. Such differences profoundly influence their relationship with the past, ownership of land, and the obligations inherited from their ancestors.

Arms and the Defence of the Dwellings

The Khazâd possess military traditions adapted to their constitution and the territories they defend. Their warriors employ axes, hammers, maces, swords, spears, and various polearms, while throwing weapons and crossbows may also find a place according to the equipment and customs of their Houses. Their mastery of metallurgy enables them to manufacture protective equipment of high quality, from helmets and shields to coats of mail and heavy armour. Their robust constitution and endurance favour fighting in close formation, particularly when defending a gate, holding a narrow passage, or resisting taller adversaries. These qualities nevertheless demand precise training, for the effectiveness of a company depends as much upon collective discipline as upon the individual strength of its warriors.

The defence of underground cities makes use of the mountain's natural features. Narrow passages limit the number of attackers, reinforced doors protect entrances, and secondary routes allow defenders to move their forces between different districts. Barriers, obstacles, and sealed passages may transform an ordinary gallery into a defensive position, particularly when engineers know the surroundings and have time to prepare. Captains must nevertheless attend to reserves, the supply of their fighters, and the security of abandoned galleries that might offer the enemy another route. A fortress may possess remarkable walls and still remain vulnerable if its inhabitants lack provisions or communication between its districts is interrupted.

Wars against the Orcs occupy a particularly important place in the memory of the Khazâd. Invasions, attacks upon mines, and battles fought for control of the mountains have caused many losses and forced several communities to abandon their homes. The memory of these conflicts sustains deep hostility, particularly among families whose ancestors were killed or driven from their lands. Dragons represent a different danger, for their power, resistance, and attraction to accumulated treasures have brought ruin upon several Dwarven settlements. Against such creatures, even the quality of armour and the strength of gates may prove insufficient, and sovereigns must sometimes choose between defending a prestigious treasure and ensuring the survival of their people.

Military life nevertheless differs greatly between individuals. A craftsman who has always lived in a peaceful dwelling may have received only elementary training to help defend his community, while a passage guard or veteran of the wars against the Orcs possesses extensive combat experience. Some Khazâd devote their lives to maintaining weapons and fortifications without personally taking part in battles, while others accompany caravans or watch over trade routes. A Dwarven character may therefore possess the physical qualities of his people without necessarily being an accomplished warrior, and the military skills he develops must remain consistent with his upbringing and the events in which he has participated.

The Rings and the Temptations of the Shadow

The Khazâd possess remarkable resistance to attempts to dominate their wills. Their nature makes them difficult to subjugate through methods employed against other peoples, as shown by the history of the Seven Rings of Power given to the Dwarf-lords. Sauron hoped to use these Rings to extend his authority, but he could not reduce their bearers to servitude as he did the nine human lords who became the Nazgûl. The Dwarves retained their own wills, although the Rings exercised a profound influence upon their desires and ambitions. In particular, they helped increase their longing for wealth and encouraged the accumulation of great treasures, whose possession gave rise to rivalries and attracted formidable enemies.

This history reminds us that their resistance to domination does not protect them against every form of corruption. Attachment to their works may become obsessive when possession takes precedence over the needs of the living, while the desire to preserve an inheritance may lead to reckless undertakings. A mine chief may continue a dangerous operation in pursuit of a lost vein, a sovereign may lead his people into war to recover an ancestral dwelling, and a craftsman may refuse to surrender an object whose possession he regards as an unquestionable right. Ancient quarrels may likewise nourish acts of vengeance whose consequences far exceed their original causes, particularly when families pass down memories of wrongs suffered through generations.

These weaknesses are possibilities of character, rather than qualities defining all Khazâd. Their courage, patience, loyalty, and faithfulness to commitments may instead lead them to resist the Shadow for many years and protect companions to whom they have become attached. A Dwarven character may devote his life to righting an injustice, preserving threatened knowledge, or rebuilding a destroyed community, even when the benefits of his undertaking will become apparent only after many years. His relationship with wealth may be equally varied: some take great pleasure in possessing precious objects, while others appreciate their craftsmanship, beauty, or usefulness more highly. A Khazâd may also be generous, preferring to give a remarkable work to a friend rather than lock it away in a treasury where no one could enjoy it.

The magical traditions of the Khazâd remain distinctive. Their heritage is primarily associated with the crafts of Mahal and the knowledge acquired by artisans, but some lineages have developed rarer practices and teachings, particularly in the material presented by MERP. In MERP-UI, access to Professions and spell lists depends upon Culture, the instruction received, and the restrictions associated with the different Dwarven magical traditions. The natural resistance of their Race and the quality of their works must therefore not be confused with any spontaneous mastery of the magical arts, whose requirements for learning remain those defined by RMU rules.

Playing a Khazâd

Playing a Khazâd in Middle-earth means portraying a character whose identity is rooted in a family, a House, and a history often far older than himself. His ancestry grants him a robust constitution, a long life, and particular dispositions, but his upbringing determines the knowledge he actually possesses. A young Dwarf may have grown up within a prosperous city, surrounded by craftsmen and experienced masters whose work gives rhythm to the daily life of his community. He knows the principal halls of his dwelling, the workshops of his kindred, and the rules governing movement through the galleries. His departure may be prompted by the desire to learn a trade under a foreign master, conclude a commercial agreement, or discover the lands described by travellers. He may also have received a specific mission from his family, particularly when a settlement wishes to strengthen its relations with other peoples or seek materials that have become difficult to obtain.

Another character may belong to a family of exiles. His ancestors abandoned a ruined mine, lost a fortress, or left a settlement that had become too dangerous, taking with them the objects and documents they could save. He has grown up among stories of that vanished dwelling, knows the names of its former sovereigns, and perhaps preserves a map, key, or tool handed down through generations. His childhood was shaped by the memory of a place he has never seen, but whose descriptions have become familiar to him. Recovering his family's former property may become the principal work of his life, particularly when he believes earlier generations endured exile in the hope that their descendants might one day return. During his travels, however, he may discover that the dwelling has changed, that other populations have settled there, or that the resources required to rebuild it exceed those available to his family.

A Dwarf-woman from a great House may wish to practise her trade far from the family workshops, represent her clan's interests in negotiations, or accompany an expedition sent to investigate a new mineral deposit. She may have learned to maintain the records of an enterprise, recognise the workmanship of different workshops, and understand the obligations attached to commercial contracts. Her departure may be welcomed by her relatives when it serves the community's needs, but give rise to greater reservations if it takes her away from home for a long time or from responsibilities already entrusted to her. Another may belong to a family whose activities developed through contact with Men and possess extensive knowledge of their languages, markets, and customs. Her experience allows her to occupy a place different from that of Dwarves who have spent their entire lives in underground settlements.

A young warrior may wish to earn a reputation before taking his place among the defenders of his community. He has received military training, knows the passages leading to his home, and can recognise the signals employed by guards, but may never have participated in a real battle. His adventure may begin when he accompanies a caravan, joins a company sent to watch the mountains, or sets out to find a relative who disappeared during an expedition. The dangers he encounters will force him to measure the difference between exercises learned under his masters and situations in which he must make decisions without receiving orders. He may discover that caution and patience are sometimes more useful than strength, particularly when the safety of his companions depends upon his ability to avoid an unnecessary confrontation.

The choice of occupation is an essential source of roleplaying opportunities. A smith may regard a weapon primarily as an object of craftsmanship whose qualities and defects he can recognise, while a soldier is more interested in its effectiveness in battle. An architect examines the bridges, gates, and defences of the cities he passes through, seeking to understand the techniques employed by their builders. A merchant familiar with dealings among Men may be more accommodating than relatives who remained in the mountains, particularly when he has learned to recognise the value of commitments made with partners of other Races. A healer may have devoted many years to studying wounds and remedies, then discover during his travels knowledge absent from his community's traditions. These occupations give the character tangible interests that may lead him to pay attention to aspects of an adventure his companions consider secondary.

A mature Khazâd may possess particularly extensive experience. He may have practised several trades, taken part in works begun long ago, or known several successive generations of the same human family. This experience enriches his relationships with other peoples, but does not mean he has mastered every discipline. A craftsman may have spent a hundred years perfecting his work while knowing little of foreign languages and military customs, while an experienced merchant may know several kingdoms without possessing the skills necessary for mining. A younger character, by contrast, may be discovering the vast outside world for the first time and begin to appreciate how greatly the traditions of his House differ from those of other inhabitants of Middle-earth. The long life of the Dwarves thus offers very different roleplaying possibilities according to the chosen age and the experiences already undergone.

The relationship with one's word and commitments may give rise to particularly rich situations. A Khazâd may regard a promise as a personal duty even when his companions believe it has lost all importance. He may feel profound gratitude towards a stranger who came to his aid, or remain attached to a family quarrel whose origins he scarcely knows. Such inclinations may lead him to pursue a difficult undertaking despite the objections of those closest to him, particularly when he believes that the honour of his House depends upon fidelity to an ancient commitment. They may also contribute to remarkably strong friendships, founded upon trust earned through shared ordeals. A character may therefore remain reserved towards foreign companions for a long time, then grant them a loyalty that no ordinary hardship will be enough to shake.

These traditions should not, however, confine the Khazâd to a single temperament. Some are austere and reserved, while others delight in feasts, songs, jokes, and the company of friends. A character may be generous with his possessions, reckless in his undertakings, curious about foreign languages, or indifferent to accumulating wealth. He may enjoy delicate craftsmanship without wishing to spend his life in a workshop, or prefer travel to the responsibilities his family intended for him. His heritage provides references and knowledge, but his decisions determine his personality. A Dwarf may deeply respect the traditions of his House while refusing to continue an ancient conflict, while another seeks to preserve his ancestors' rights with a stubbornness that eventually damages his relationships with his companions.

Differences between the Houses also offer many possibilities. A Longbeard may remain deeply attached to the memory of Khazad-dûm, particularly when his family preserves stories of a settlement it was forced to abandon. A descendant of the ancient cities of the Blue Mountains may maintain traditions associated with relations with the Elves of Beleriand, whose consequences continue to influence the agreements or grievances of certain families. A Dwarf from the eastern regions may belong to a community whose customs are almost unknown to the peoples of the West and discover during his travels that his companions are chiefly familiar with the traditions of the House of Durin. The Cultures developed by MERP thus allow characters to possess distinct historical and social origins without altering the fundamental qualities they share as Khazâd.

A character may also be compelled to leave his home for reasons beyond his control. War, the exhaustion of a mine, the closure of a trade route, or a family dispute may threaten the activities to which he has devoted his life. A craftsman may have to seek new patrons, a merchant may lose the agreements upon which his enterprise depended, and a young Dwarf may be sent to another House to continue his apprenticeship. These circumstances provide many concrete reasons to undertake a journey and join companions from other peoples. Adventure may then become a means of finding resources, preserving knowledge, or preparing the rebuilding of a threatened community.

Relationships with other Races offer numerous opportunities for the character to develop. A Dwarf may have grown up hearing tales of ancient quarrels with the Elves and discover during his travels individuals whose knowledge and courage deserve his esteem. A merchant accustomed to dealings with Men may become attached to a family whose successive generations he has known, while a young warrior may be surprised by the speed with which his human companions grow old. Hobbits may seem little concerned with great undertakings until he discovers their courage and attachment to ordinary things.
